claim: Pheromone communication mediates the social hierarchy, division of labor, and concerted activities of colony members in eusocial insect societies.
source: Pheromone communication is the cornerstone of eusocial insect societies since it mediates the social hierarchy, division of labor, and concerted activities of colony members.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about eusocial insect biology.

claim: No odorant receptor (OR) has been functionally characterized in termites prior to this study.
source: The current knowledge on molecular mechanisms of social insect pheromone detection by odorant receptors (ORs) is limited to bees and ants, while no OR was yet functionally characterized in termites, the oldest eusocial insect clade.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field prior to the current work.

claim: Four OR sequences from Prorhinotermes simplex were selected for functional characterization.
source: We selected four OR sequences from the annotated antennal transcriptome of the termite Prorhinotermes simplex (Psammotermitidae), expressed them in Empty Neuron Drosophila, and functionally characterized them using single sensillum recording (SSR).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach taken in the study.

claim: PsimOR14 responds strongly to neocembrene, the main component of P. simplex trail-following pheromone.
source: For one of the selected ORs, PsimOR14, we obtained strong responses to the main component of P. simplex trail-following pheromone, the monocyclic diterpene neocembrene.
evidence: This is a primary finding from SSR experiments reported in the manuscript.

claim: PsimOR14 shows narrow tuning to neocembrene with only one additional compound out of 67 tested generating non-negligible responses.
source: PsimOR14 showed a narrow tuning to neocembrene with only one additional compound out of 67 tested generating non-negligible responses.
evidence: This is based on SSR screening data with multiple chemical panels.

claim: PsimOR14 is significantly more expressed in worker antennae compared to soldiers.
source: Finally, we demonstrate that PsimOR14 is significantly more expressed in worker antennae compared to soldiers, which correlates with higher sensitivity of workers to neocembrene.
evidence: This is based on differential expression analysis of RNAseq data.

claim: Workers show higher sensitivity to neocembrene compared to soldiers.
source: Finally, we demonstrate that PsimOR14 is significantly more expressed in worker antennae compared to soldiers, which correlates with higher sensitivity of workers to neocembrene.
evidence: This is based on EAG measurements comparing the two castes.

claim: Ants and termites show many similarities in chemical signaling despite great evolutionary distance.
source: The convergent evolution of chemical signaling is best manifested by many similarities between ants and termites, in spite of the great evolutionary distance between these two dominant groups of social insects with great ecological significance (Leonhardt et al., 2016; Tuma et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The multigene family of insect odorant receptors was identified in Drosophila melanogaster.
source: Since the identification of the multigene family of insect odorant receptors (ORs) expressed in antennae and maxillary palps of Drosophila melanogaster (Clyne et al., 1999), neurophysiology of insect olfaction has seen great progress in terms of phylogenetic reconstructions of OR evolution across taxa, functional characterizations (deorphanizations) of multiple ORs and ultimately their recent structural characterizations (Butterwick et al., 2018; Del Mármol et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Clyne et al., 1999.

claim: Insect ORs have an inverted membrane topology compared to vertebrate ORs.
source: Insect ORs have an inverted membrane topology in the dendrites of olfactory sensory neurons compared to vertebrate ORs (Benton et al., 2006; Clyne et al., 1999) and unlike the vertebrate ORs known to act as GPCR receptors, insect ORs function as odorant-gated ion channels (Sato et al., 2008; Wicher et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Insect ORs function as odorant-gated ion channels.
source: Insect ORs have an inverted membrane topology in the dendrites of olfactory sensory neurons compared to vertebrate ORs (Benton et al., 2006; Clyne et al., 1999) and unlike the vertebrate ORs known to act as GPCR receptors, insect ORs function as odorant-gated ion channels (Sato et al., 2008; Wicher et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sato et al., 2008 and Wicher et al., 2008.

claim: ORs from basal wingless insect lineage Archaeognatha are homotetramers.
source: While the ORs from the basal wingless insect lineage Archaeognatha are homotetramers (Del Mármol et al., 2021; Brand et al., 2018), ORs of all other Insecta form heteromeric complexes with a highly conserved coreceptor protein (ORCo) (Brand et al., 2018; Butterwick et al., 2018; Larsson et al., 2004; Sato et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Del Mármol et al., 2021 and Brand et al., 2018.

claim: ORs of all Insecta except Archaeognatha form heteromeric complexes with ORCo.
source: While the ORs from the basal wingless insect lineage Archaeognatha are homotetramers (Del Mármol et al., 2021; Brand et al., 2018), ORs of all other Insecta form heteromeric complexes with a highly conserved coreceptor protein (ORCo) (Brand et al., 2018; Butterwick et al., 2018; Larsson et al., 2004; Sato et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: OR-ORCo complexes in mosquitoes and aphids consist of one OR and three ORCo subunits.
source: As recently shown in mosquitoes and aphids, these complexes consist of one OR and three ORCo subunits (Wang et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wang et al., 2024 and Zhao et al., 2024.

claim: The OR repertoire varies greatly across Insecta, ranging from units to hundreds of ORs.
source: The OR repertoire is greatly variable across Insecta and ranges from units in the wingless Archaeognatha and basal winged order Odonata to tens or hundreds ORs identified in most other flying insects (Robertson, 2019; Yan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Robertson, 2019 and Yan et al., 2020.

claim: The OR family evolved via rapid birth-and-death process with multiple gene duplications, pseudogenizations, and losses.
source: Insect ORs often lack a clear orthology pattern across phylogeny, because the OR family evolved via rapid birth-and-death process, accompanied by multiple gene duplications, pseudogenizations, and losses.
evidence: This is established knowledge about OR evolution.

claim: Lineage-specific expansions and variability in OR ligand specificities allow for rapid response of olfactory system to ecological and life history changes.
source: Lineage-specific expansions, together with a considerable variability in OR ligand specificities (from broad to narrow tuning), allow for a rapid response of olfactory system to ecological and life history changes (Andersson et al., 2015; Benton, 2015; Nei and Rooney, 2005; Robertson, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Specialist insects often have lower repertoires of ORs compared to generalist insects.
source: Ecology-driven plasticity in OR evolution has been convincingly demonstrated by comparisons of specialist versus generalist insects, the former often having much lower repertoires of ORs and other chemosensory proteins (Robertson, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Robertson, 2019.

claim: Multiple ORs have been deorphanized in ants and honey bees.
source: Within social insects, eusocial Hymenoptera received considerable attention both in terms of OR repertoire reconstructions and functional characterizations with multiple ORs being deorphanized in ants (Pask et al., 2017; Slone et al., 2017) and the honey bee (e.g., Gomez Ramirez et al., 2023; Wanner et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The 9-exon subfamily in ants and paper wasps participates in detection of cuticular hydrocarbons.
source: The amassed knowledge suggests that the complex communication and orientation capabilities in the colonies of eusocial Hymenoptera are facilitated by the greatly expanded repertoire of ORs, especially that of the 9-exon subfamily in ants and paper wasps participating in the detection of cuticular hydrocarbons (CHCs) as important cues in contact chemoreception of colony and caste identity and fertility status in eusocial insects (Engsontia et al., 2015; Legan et al., 2021; McKenzie et al., 2016; Pask et al., 2017; Zhou et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The 9-exon subfamily and overall OR richness were inherited by extant eusocial Hymenoptera from the ancestor of Aculeata.
source: The 9-exon subfamily and the overall OR richness have been inherited by the extant eusocial Hymenoptera from the ancestor of Aculeata (McKenzie et al., 2016), and also solitary aculeate taxa display large OR repertoires Obiero et al., 2021; this preadaptation might have been important for the repeated emergence of eusociality and the related complex communication.
evidence: This is supported by citation to McKenzie et al., 2016.

claim: Parasitic ant taxa show reduction of OR array including 9-exon genes along with simplification of behavioral repertoire.
source: This is supported by the reduction of OR array (including 9-exon genes) in parasitic ant taxa, along with the simplification of their behavioral repertoire (Jongepier et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jongepier et al., 2022.

claim: Termite ORs range from 28 to 69 in total number.
source: Termite ORs are organized in relatively conserved, highly orthologous pattern, and their total numbers range from 28 to 69 (Johny et al., 2023; Terrapon et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Johny et al., 2023 and Terrapon et al., 2014.

claim: Termites have lower numbers of ORs than their solitary cockroach relative Blattella germanica.
source: These numbers are lower than in their solitary cockroach relative Blattella germanica (Harrison et al., 2018), and dramatically lower than in ants, having up to over 400 ORs (Engsontia et al., 2015; Legan et al., 2021; McKenzie et al., 2016; Pask et al., 2017; Zhou et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Harrison et al., 2018 and multiple ant studies.

claim: Ants have up to over 400 ORs.
source: These numbers are lower than in their solitary cockroach relative Blattella germanica (Harrison et al., 2018), and dramatically lower than in ants, having up to over 400 ORs (Engsontia et al., 2015; Legan et al., 2021; McKenzie et al., 2016; Pask et al., 2017; Zhou et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Termites contradict the paradigm on eusociality as a driver of OR richness.
source: Thus, termites clearly contradict the paradigm on eusociality as a driver of OR richness, even though their chemical communication is by far more complex than in solitary insects and includes pheromone components from a variety of chemical classes, such as fatty-acyl derived alcohols, aldehydes and ketones, terpenoids, and, last but not least, the CHCs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of OR numbers between termites and ants.

claim: Termites independently evolved an intricate communication system using CHCs as kin- and nestmate discrimination cues and as indicators of caste identity and fertility status.
source: Independently of eusocial Hymenoptera, termites evolved an intricate communication system using CHCs as kin- and nestmate discrimination cues and as indicators of caste identity and fertility status (reviewed in Bagnères and Hanus, 2015; Mitaka and Akino, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: Termites possess an extraordinarily rich set of ionotropic receptors (IRs), reaching up to more than 100 in some species.
source: One of the alternative hypotheses springs from observations that termites possess an extraordinarily rich set of ionotropic receptors (IRs), reaching up to more than 100 in some species (Harrison et al., 2018; Johny et al., 2023; Terrapon et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Blattella germanica has the largest IR repertoire ever identified in insects.
source: Even though the richness of IRs is shared by termites and their cockroach relatives, with B. germanica having the largest IR repertoire ever identified in insects (Robertson et al., 2018), IRs also underwent termite-specific expansions (Harrison et al., 2018; Johny et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Robertson et al., 2018.

claim: IRs underwent termite-specific expansions.
source: Even though the richness of IRs is shared by termites and their cockroach relatives, with B. germanica having the largest IR repertoire ever identified in insects (Robertson et al., 2018), IRs also underwent termite-specific expansions (Harrison et al., 2018; Johny et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Harrison et al., 2018 and Johny et al., 2023.

claim: Insect IRs have been shown to respond to volatile ligands.
source: Since insect IRs have been shown to respond to volatile ligands (Benton et al., 2009), we cannot rule out that they also participate in the complex chemical communication in termites, as has been previously speculated (Harrison et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Benton et al., 2009.

claim: The majority of termite OR sequences are organized into two large sister clusters in the phylogenetic tree.
source: In the resulting tree, all ORCo sequences and ORs from L. saccharina were basally situated, while the majority of termite OR sequences were organized into two large sister clusters, both of which were further split into several sub-branches mostly containing one sequence from all five termite species (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic reconstruction shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Termite ORs show a highly orthologous pattern with mostly one sequence from all five termite species in each sub-branch.
source: In the resulting tree, all ORCo sequences and ORs from L. saccharina were basally situated, while the majority of termite OR sequences were organized into two large sister clusters, both of which were further split into several sub-branches mostly containing one sequence from all five termite species (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic reconstruction shown in Figure 1A.

claim: 26 out of 50 ORs identified in P. simplex represent full open reading frames with at least 6 transmembrane domains.
source: Out of the 50 ORs identified in P. simplex, 26 sequences represented full open reading frames with at least 6 undisputed transmembrane domains predicted using TMHMM-2.0.
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis of OR sequences.

claim: Four P. simplex ORs (PsimOR9, 14, 30, and 31) were selected for transgenic D. melanogaster generation and SSR screening.
source: From these, we selected four sequences (PsimOR9, 14, 30, and 31) situated in different parts (sub-branches) of the tree (Figure 1) and used them for transgenic D. melanogaster generation and SSR screening.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Spontaneous SSR firing rates of the four transgenic lines showed an expected pattern with no abnormal bursts.
source: Spontaneous SSR firing rates of the four transgenic lines showed an expected pattern with no abnormal bursts, indicating that the ORs were functional.
evidence: This is based on SSR measurements.

claim: PsimOR9 and PsimOR30 did not provide any strong response to any of the tested compounds in Panel 1.
source: As shown in Figure 2A, PsimOR9 and PsimOR30 did not provide any strong response to any of the tested compounds, and PsimOR31 broadly and weakly responded to several compounds.
evidence: This is based on SSR screening data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: PsimOR31 broadly and weakly responded to several compounds in Panel 1.
source: As shown in Figure 2A, PsimOR9 and PsimOR30 did not provide any strong response to any of the tested compounds, and PsimOR31 broadly and weakly responded to several compounds.
evidence: This is based on SSR screening data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: PsimOR14 systematically and strongly responded to stimulations by neocembrene.
source: By contrast, PsimOR14 systematically and strongly responded to stimulations by the monocyclic diterpene hydrocarbon neocembrene, which is the main component of the TFP in the genus Prorhinotermes (Sillam-Dussès et al., 2009).
evidence: This is based on SSR screening data.

claim: Neocembrene is the main component of the trail-following pheromone in the genus Prorhinotermes.
source: By contrast, PsimOR14 systematically and strongly responded to stimulations by the monocyclic diterpene hydrocarbon neocembrene, which is the main component of the TFP in the genus Prorhinotermes (Sillam-Dussès et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sillam-Dussès et al., 2009.

claim: PsimOR14 showed a moderate response to geranylgeraniol.
source: Additionally, a moderate PsimOR14 response was also recorded for the linear diterpene alcohol geranylgeraniol, while all other compounds in the panel, including two other terpenoids, only elicited weak or no responses (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on SSR screening data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: All other compounds in Panel 1 except neocembrene and geranylgeraniol only elicited weak or no responses from PsimOR14.
source: Additionally, a moderate PsimOR14 response was also recorded for the linear diterpene alcohol geranylgeraniol, while all other compounds in the panel, including two other terpenoids, only elicited weak or no responses (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on SSR screening data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The W1118 ab3 sensillum did not show any significant neuronal response to Panel 1 compounds.
source: As evidenced in Figure 2B, the W1118 ab3 sensillum did not show any significant neuronal response to Panel 1 compounds, while the transgenic PsimOR14 line generated an average Δ spike number of >50 spikes/s for neocembrene and a minor secondary response of ~25 Δ spikes/s for geranylgeraniol.
evidence: This is based on SSR comparison data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The transgenic PsimOR14 line generated an average Δ spike number of >50 spikes/s for neocembrene.
source: As evidenced in Figure 2B, the W1118 ab3 sensillum did not show any significant neuronal response to Panel 1 compounds, while the transgenic PsimOR14 line generated an average Δ spike number of >50 spikes/s for neocembrene and a minor secondary response of ~25 Δ spikes/s for geranylgeraniol.
evidence: This is based on SSR comparison data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The transgenic PsimOR14 line generated a minor secondary response of ~25 Δ spikes/s for geranylgeraniol.
source: As evidenced in Figure 2B, the W1118 ab3 sensillum did not show any significant neuronal response to Panel 1 compounds, while the transgenic PsimOR14 line generated an average Δ spike number of >50 spikes/s for neocembrene and a minor secondary response of ~25 Δ spikes/s for geranylgeraniol.
evidence: This is based on SSR comparison data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: PsimOR14 shows an exponentially increasing neuronal response to neocembrene over the range of 0.01–10 ng with ED50 = ~24 ng.
source: In the next step, we tested the dose–response behavior of PsimOR14 flies to neocembrene and recorded an exponentially increasing neuronal response over the range of 0.01–10 ng to ED50 = ~24 ng and a lack of saturation at the dose of 500 ng (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is based on dose-response experiments shown in Figure 2D.

claim: PsimOR14 response to neocembrene lacks saturation at the dose of 500 ng.
source: In the next step, we tested the dose–response behavior of PsimOR14 flies to neocembrene and recorded an exponentially increasing neuronal response over the range of 0.01–10 ng to ED50 = ~24 ng and a lack of saturation at the dose of 500 ng (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is based on dose-response experiments shown in Figure 2D.

claim: None of the 56 compounds in Panels 2-4 generated a strong response from PsimOR14.
source: To further address the specificity of PsimOR14 tuning, we tested three additional panels containing 56 frequently occurring insect semiochemicals from various chemical classes. As shown in Figure 3A, none of these compounds, including multiple terpenoids (mono-, sesqui-, di-), generated a strong response, suggesting a narrow tuning of PsimOR14 to neocembrene.
evidence: This is based on SSR screening data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: PsimOR14 has a receptor lifetime sparseness value of 0.88.
source: The narrow tuning of PsimOR14 is evident also from the tuning curve depicted in Figure 3B, with the receptor lifetime sparseness value 0.88.
evidence: This is based on analysis of SSR data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: PsimOR14 is a pheromone receptor adaptively tuned to detect the main TFP component, neocembrene.
source: These results confirm that PsimOR14 is a pheromone receptor adaptively tuned to detect the main TFP component, neocembrene.
evidence: This is an inference based on the narrow tuning and strong response to neocembrene.

claim: A short multiporous grooved sensillum in the apical part of the last antennal segment of P. simplex workers responds strongly to neocembrene and geranylgeraniol.
source: In SSR experiments with the termite-relevant compounds from Panel 1, we obtained strong response to both neocembrene and geranylgeraniol from a short multiporous grooved sensillum situated in the apical part of the last antennal segment (Figure 4A, B).
evidence: This is based on SSR measurements on termite antennae shown in Figure 4.

claim: The neocembrene-responding sensillum shows three different spike amplitudes suggesting the presence of three olfactory sensory neurons.
source: Detailed view on spontaneous firing pattern of the neocembrene-responding sensillum revealed three different spike amplitudes (Figure 4C), suggesting the potential presence of as many as three olfactory sensory neurons (a–c).
evidence: This is based on analysis of SSR traces shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The responses to neocembrene and geranylgeraniol in the termite sensillum are generated by neuron b.
source: Comparison with spike amplitudes upon neocembrene and geranylgeraniol stimulations then indicated that the responses are generated by the neuron labeled as b.
evidence: This is based on comparison of spike amplitudes in SSR traces.

claim: The SSR response spectrum of neocembrene sensillum to Panel 1 is markedly similar to that of ab3A neuron of PsimOR14-expressing Drosophila.
source: The SSR response spectrum of neocembrene sensillum to Panel 1 was markedly similar to that of ab3A neuron of PsimOR14-expressing Drosophila (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is based on comparison of SSR data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The neocembrene sensillum in P. simplex workers shows average Δ spikes/s of ~65 for neocembrene and ~29 for geranylgeraniol.
source: None of the compounds elicited higher average responses than 10 Δ spikes/s, except for neocembrene and geranylgeraniol; their average Δ spikes/s were even slightly higher than those of heterologously expressed PsimOR14, reaching ~65 and ~29, respectively (Figure 5A, B).
evidence: This is based on SSR measurements shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: The neocembrene-detecting sensillum in P. simplex workers shows a dose-response to neocembrene with ED50 = 0.016 ng.
source: Likewise, the dose–response experiment with neocembrene indicated a higher sensitivity threshold and lower ED50 = 0.016 ng (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is based on dose-response experiments shown in Figure 5C.

claim: PsimOR14 gene consists of six exons.
source: Mapping the PsimOR14 transcript sequence on P. simplex draft genome revealed that the gene consists of six exons and is situated on the same locus and in close vicinity of PsimOR15, with which it shares the exon-intron boundaries, suggesting a recent diversification of the two genes via duplication, as also supported by their high sequence similarity (Figure 1A and Figure 6A).
evidence: This is based on genomic mapping shown in Figure 6A.

claim: PsimOR14 is situated on the same locus and in close vicinity of PsimOR15.
source: Mapping the PsimOR14 transcript sequence on P. simplex draft genome revealed that the gene consists of six exons and is situated on the same locus and in close vicinity of PsimOR15, with which it shares the exon-intron boundaries, suggesting a recent diversification of the two genes via duplication, as also supported by their high sequence similarity (Figure 1A and Figure 6A).
evidence: This is based on genomic mapping shown in Figure 6A.

claim: PsimOR14 and PsimOR15 share exon-intron boundaries, suggesting recent diversification via duplication.
source: Mapping the PsimOR14 transcript sequence on P. simplex draft genome revealed that the gene consists of six exons and is situated on the same locus and in close vicinity of PsimOR15, with which it shares the exon-intron boundaries, suggesting a recent diversification of the two genes via duplication, as also supported by their high sequence similarity (Figure 1A and Figure 6A).
evidence: This is based on genomic mapping and phylogenetic analysis shown in Figures 1A and 6A.

claim: PsimOR14 has seven transmembrane domains (S1–S7).
source: Transcript (Figure 6B) and protein (Figure 6C) structures of PsimOR14 showed the presence of seven transmembrane domains (S1–S7) with the largest extracellular loop between S3 and S4 and the longest intracellular loop between S4 and S5.
evidence: This is based on protein structure prediction shown in Figure 6C.

claim: PsimOR14 has the largest extracellular loop between S3 and S4.
source: Transcript (Figure 6B) and protein (Figure 6C) structures of PsimOR14 showed the presence of seven transmembrane domains (S1–S7) with the largest extracellular loop between S3 and S4 and the longest intracellular loop between S4 and S5.
evidence: This is based on protein structure prediction shown in Figure 6C.

claim: PsimOR14 has the longest intracellular loop between S4 and S5.
source: Transcript (Figure 6B) and protein (Figure 6C) structures of PsimOR14 showed the presence of seven transmembrane domains (S1–S7) with the largest extracellular loop between S3 and S4 and the longest intracellular loop between S4 and S5.
evidence: This is based on protein structure prediction shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The binding site of PsimOR14 is located in a binding pocket deep in the transmembrane region.
source: Likewise, the docking experiments identified a binding site defined by a binding pocket deep in the transmembrane region, homologous to that in previously studied insect ORs, and confirmed the nature of the ligand binding to mainly rely on hydrophobic interactions (e.g., Del Mármol et al., 2021; Pettersson and Cattaneo, 2023; Yuvaraj et al., 2021).
evidence: This is based on docking experiments and comparison with other insect ORs.

claim: Ligand binding to PsimOR14 mainly relies on hydrophobic interactions.
source: Likewise, the docking experiments identified a binding site defined by a binding pocket deep in the transmembrane region, homologous to that in previously studied insect ORs, and confirmed the nature of the ligand binding to mainly rely on hydrophobic interactions (e.g., Del Mármol et al., 2021; Pettersson and Cattaneo, 2023; Yuvaraj et al., 2021).
evidence: This is based on docking experiments and supported by citations.

claim: Residues from S3 and S4 of PsimOR14 interact with the studied ligands.
source: In the case of PsimOR14, mainly the residues from S3 and S4 interacted with the studied ligands; these transmembrane domains were shown to participate in ligand binding also in other studied insect ORs (e.g., Del Mármol et al., 2021; Yuvaraj et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2024).
evidence: This is based on docking experiments and supported by citations.

claim: The calculated binding scores for the three tested ligands correlated with observed biological effects.
source: The calculated binding scores for the three tested ligands correlated with observed biological effects of the ligands.
evidence: This is based on comparison of docking scores with SSR data.

claim: MM/PBSA analysis estimated (+)-limonene as the worst agonist.
source: The MM/PBSA data also in part corroborated the SSR measurements by estimating (+)-limonene as the worst agonist; by contrast, geranylgeraniol and not neocembrene ranked as the best ligand.
evidence: This is based on MM/PBSA calculations.

claim: MM/PBSA analysis ranked geranylgeraniol as the best ligand for PsimOR14.
source: The MM/PBSA data also in part corroborated the SSR measurements by estimating (+)-limonene as the worst agonist; by contrast, geranylgeraniol and not neocembrene ranked as the best ligand.
evidence: This is based on MM/PBSA calculations.

claim: All three tested ligands bind two hydrophobic patches made of residues from S3 and S4 of PsimOR14.
source: Per-residue decomposition results (Figure 6C) showed that all three ligands bind two hydrophobic patches made out of residues from S3 and S4 (Cys154, Ala157, Val158; Thr221, Leu224, Ala225, Tyr228).
evidence: This is based on per-residue decomposition analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Geranylgeraniol interacts with additional residues of PsimOR14 beyond the two hydrophobic patches.
source: Neocembrene and (+)-limonene only bind these patches, while geranylgeraniol also interacts with additional residues (Figure 6—source data 2).
evidence: This is based on per-residue decomposition analysis.

claim: Binding of the three tested ligands reduces the overall protein dynamicity of PsimOR14.
source: MD simulations of per atom explored volumes in PsimOR14 apoform and upon ligand binding delimited three regions with high dynamicity, that is the N-terminal region, the extracellular S3 and S4 loops, and especially the intracellular S4 and S5 loop (Figure 6F). Binding of each of the three ligands reduced the overall protein dynamicity; this protein stabilization did not differ dramatically among the three ligands.
evidence: This is based on MD simulations shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Binding of geranylgeraniol and neocembrene leads to a conspicuous dynamicity increase in a portion of the S4 and S5 loop of PsimOR14.
source: By contrast, binding of geranylgeraniol and neocembrene led to a conspicuous dynamicity increase in a portion of the S4 and S5 loop, compared to both the apoform and (+)-limonene binding (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is based on MD simulations shown in Figure 6G.

claim: PsimOR14 is among the three most upregulated ORs in workers compared to soldiers.
source: Both DESeq2 and EdgeR differential expression analyses of RNAseq read counts from heads (including antennae) of workers and soldiers revealed that PsimOR14 is significantly more expressed in workers, being among the three most upregulated ORs in workers (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is based on differential expression analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Workers show significantly stronger EAG responses to neocembrene than soldiers (p = 0.012).
source: Subsequent electroantennographic (EAG) measurements were in line with this observation and indicated significantly stronger responses to neocembrene in workers (p = 0.012) (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is based on EAG measurements shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Identification of PsimOR14 as the pheromone receptor tuned to neocembrene represents the first OR deorphanization in termites.
source: Identification of PsimOR14 as the pheromone receptor narrowly tuned to neocembrene in P. simplex represents the first OR deorphanization in termites and confirms that the trail-following communication is mediated by ORs.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main finding.

claim: Trail-following communication in termites is mediated by ORs.
source: Identification of PsimOR14 as the pheromone receptor narrowly tuned to neocembrene in P. simplex represents the first OR deorphanization in termites and confirms that the trail-following communication is mediated by ORs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the identification of PsimOR14 as a neocembrene receptor.

claim: ORCo silencing in two termite species having a C12 fatty alcohol as TFP impaired the ability to follow the foraging trail.
source: This assumption, validated here for the monocyclic diterpene neocembrene, is indirectly supported by previous experiments in two termite species having a C12 fatty alcohol as TFP; ORCo silencing in these species impaired the ability to follow the foraging trail (Gao et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gao et al., 2020.

claim: Trail following and courtship communication in termites have shared evolutionary origin.
source: Because trail following in termites has the shared evolutionary origin with courtship communication and both neocembrene and C12 alcohols also occur as sex-pairing pheromone components (Bagnères and Hanus, 2015; Bordereau and Pasteels, 2011; Sillam-Dussès, 2010), it is likely that the two communication modalities share identical or closely related ORs.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Neocembrene and C12 alcohols occur as sex-pairing pheromone components in termites.
source: Because trail following in termites has the shared evolutionary origin with courtship communication and both neocembrene and C12 alcohols also occur as sex-pairing pheromone components (Bagnères and Hanus, 2015; Bordereau and Pasteels, 2011; Sillam-Dussès, 2010), it is likely that the two communication modalities share identical or closely related ORs.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Trail following and sex attraction in termites likely share identical or closely related ORs.
source: Because trail following in termites has the shared evolutionary origin with courtship communication and both neocembrene and C12 alcohols also occur as sex-pairing pheromone components (Bagnères and Hanus, 2015; Bordereau and Pasteels, 2011; Sillam-Dussès, 2010), it is likely that the two communication modalities share identical or closely related ORs.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the shared evolutionary origin and chemical components.

claim: PsimOR14 has spontaneous firing rates of 6.87 ± 4.73 Hz (mean ± SD).
source: Neurophysiological characteristics of D. melanogaster ab3A neuron expressing PsimOR14 showed expected patterns of spontaneous firing rates of units of Hz (6.87 ± 4.73, mean ± SD) and maximum firing rates of 90 spikes/s at the highest used neocembrene doses (1 µg), though not reaching the reported maxima for ab3A responses with genuine and exogenous receptors, which may be well over 100 spikes/s (e.g., Chahda et al., 2019).
evidence: This is based on SSR measurements.

claim: PsimOR14 shows maximum firing rates of 90 spikes/s at 1 µg neocembrene dose.
source: Neurophysiological characteristics of D. melanogaster ab3A neuron expressing PsimOR14 showed expected patterns of spontaneous firing rates of units of Hz (6.87 ± 4.73, mean ± SD) and maximum firing rates of 90 spikes/s at the highest used neocembrene doses (1 µg), though not reaching the reported maxima for ab3A responses with genuine and exogenous receptors, which may be well over 100 spikes/s (e.g., Chahda et al., 2019).
evidence: This is based on SSR measurements.

claim: Co-expression of termite ORs with Drosophila ORCo using the Empty Neuron system is a suitable technique for termite OR characterizations.
source: This confirms that co-expression of termite ORs with the Drosophila ORCo using the Empty Neuron system is a suitable technique for termite OR characterizations.
evidence: This is an inference based on the successful functional characterization of PsimOR14.

claim: ORs detecting pheromone components and other volatiles with high biological importance are often expressed in specialized sensilla and are highly selective.
source: ORs detecting pheromone components (pheromone receptors) and other volatiles with high biological importance, such as key food or host attractants, are often expressed in specialized sensilla and are highly selective, in contrast to the broad tuning of ORs sensing the general environmental stimuli (e.g., Carey et al., 2010; Fleischer and Krieger, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Sex pheromone receptors in moths are mostly tuned to a single compound.
source: Such a high selectivity is the best known for sex pheromone receptors, for example in moths (reviewed in Zhang and Löfstedt, 2015) or Drosophila (reviewed in Haverkamp et al., 2018), mostly tuned to a single compound, even though in some cases the respective ORs can be adaptively shaped to selectively detect more pheromone compounds (Díaz-Morales et al., 2024; Mariette et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citations to review articles and specific studies.

claim: The narrow tuning of PsimOR14 is in line with expectations from a pheromone receptor.
source: Thus, the narrow tuning of PsimOR14 is in line with expectations from a pheromone receptor, especially when considering the ancient origin of trail-following from sex-pairing behavior and the great importance of TFP for concerted foraging in these blind insects.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with known pheromone receptors.

claim: Geranylgeraniol was the only other agonist with non-negligible response (average Δ spike/s over 20) for PsimOR14.
source: With average Δ spike/s over 20, the linear diterpene alcohol geranylgeraniol was the only other agonist with non-negligible response.
evidence: This is based on SSR screening data.

claim: There is no record of geranylgeraniol in communication context in termites.
source: It is difficult to attribute any adaptive significance to this observation since there is no record of geranylgeraniol in communication context in termites.
evidence: This is a statement about the lack of prior knowledge.

claim: The observed biological activity of geranylgeraniol may be due to non-adaptive binding affinity of PsimOR14 to the non-native ligand.
source: Therefore, the observed significant biological activity, high docking score, and high ranking in free energy comparison may be due to non-adaptive binding affinity of PsimOR14 to the non-native ligand (see also below).
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of geranylgeraniol binding.

claim: Linalool had the biggest negative Δ spike score (–6.8) for PsimOR14.
source: Interestingly, another related terpene alcohol, the monoterpene linalool, had the biggest negative Δ spike score (–6.8) and the absolute spikes/s ranged from 0 to 5 (1.5 ± 1.9, mean ± SD), suggesting a possible inverse agonist function of linalool.
evidence: This is based on SSR screening data.

claim: Linalool may function as an inverse agonist for PsimOR14.
source: Interestingly, another related terpene alcohol, the monoterpene linalool, had the biggest negative Δ spike score (–6.8) and the absolute spikes/s ranged from 0 to 5 (1.5 ± 1.9, mean ± SD), suggesting a possible inverse agonist function of linalool.
evidence: This is speculation based on the negative response.

claim: No important responses to the minor P. simplex TFP component (3Z,6Z,8E)-dodecatrien-1-ol were recorded from the neocembrene-detecting sensillum.
source: No other important responses to termite pheromone components from the Panel 1, which also included the minor P. simplex TFP component (3Z,6Z,8E)-dodecatrien-1-ol, were recorded, in spite of the likely presence of two additional olfactory neurons housed in the neocembrene-detecting sensillum.
evidence: This is based on SSR measurements on termite antennae.

claim: The function of the two additional neurons in the neocembrene-detecting sensillum remains elusive.
source: The function of these additional neurons remains elusive, and examples from other insects offer multiple scenarios.
evidence: This is a statement about the lack of knowledge regarding these neurons.

claim: The SSR analyses did not perform a comprehensive mapping of olfactory sensilla on the entire worker antenna.
source: However, it must be noted that our SSR analyses focused on a specific sensillum defined by its topology on the last flagellomere, and we did not perform a comprehensive mapping of olfactory sensilla on the entire worker antenna.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the study.

claim: The basic PsimOR14 protein architecture with seven transmembrane domains is typical for insect ORs.
source: The basic PsimOR14 protein architecture with seven transmembrane domains is typical for insect ORs.
evidence: This is based on protein structure prediction and comparison with known insect ORs.

claim: The binding site of PsimOR14 is homologous to that in previously studied insect ORs.
source: Likewise, the docking experiments identified a binding site defined by a binding pocket deep in the transmembrane region, homologous to that in previously studied insect ORs, and confirmed the nature of the ligand binding to mainly rely on hydrophobic interactions (e.g., Del Mármol et al., 2021; Pettersson and Cattaneo, 2023; Yuvaraj et al., 2021).
evidence: This is based on docking experiments and comparison with other insect ORs.

claim: S3 and S4 transmembrane domains participate in ligand binding in other studied insect ORs.
source: In the case of PsimOR14, mainly the residues from S3 and S4 interacted with the studied ligands; these transmembrane domains were shown to participate in ligand binding also in other studied insect ORs (e.g., Del Mármol et al., 2021; Yuvaraj et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Geranylgeraniol binding to PsimOR14 has a relatively higher contribution of electrostatic interactions compared to neocembrene and (+)-limonene.
source: This may potentially be explained by the additional residues interacting with geranylgeraniol compared to neocembrene and (+)-limonene, and the relatively higher contribution of electrostatic interactions in geranylgeraniol binding.
evidence: This is based on MM/PBSA analysis.

claim: In systems where ligand binding induces allosteric effects, simple binding affinity does not provide a complete picture of receptor signal transduction function.
source: Moreover, in systems where ligand binding induces allosteric effects, as is the case of insect ORs, the simple binding affinity does not provide a complete picture of receptor signal transduction function.
evidence: This is a general statement about receptor function.

claim: Some parts of the intracellular S4 and S5 loops of PsimOR14 show significant increase in dynamics upon binding of geranylgeraniol and neocembrene.
source: In contrast to the general protein stabilization upon binding of the three tested ligands, some parts of the intracellular S4 and S5 loops showed a significant increase in the dynamics upon binding of the biologically active ligands geranylgeraniol and neocembrene, compared to apoform and the weak agonist (+)-limonene binding.
evidence: This is based on MD simulations.

claim: Replacement of the S4-S5 loop with a short linker increased the receptor response to native ligand in MhOR5 from Machilis hrabei.
source: However, the impact of the S4-S5 loop on OR function has previously been reported for the MhOR5 from Machilis hrabei Del Mármol et al., 2021; replacement of the loop with a short linker increased the receptor response to native ligand.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Del Mármol et al., 2021.

claim: In some insect ORs, the S4-S5 loop has been reduced to a short sequence of a few residues.
source: Interestingly, in some insect ORs, this loop has been reduced to a short sequence of a few residues (e.g., Wang et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2024.

claim: PsimOR14 does not belong to the most expressed P. simplex ORs.
source: PsimOR14 does not belong to the most expressed P. simplex ORs (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is based on transcript abundance data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: PsimOR14 is among those ORs having the most caste-biased expression.
source: However, interestingly, it is among those having the most caste-biased expression with significantly higher transcript abundance in antennae of workers compared to soldiers.
evidence: This is based on differential expression analysis.

claim: Termite soldiers lay pheromone trails, detect TFPs and participate in foraging in a number of termite species.
source: Termite soldiers are known to lay pheromone trails, to detect TFPs and to participate in foraging and field exploration in a number of termite species, though the behavioral patterns of soldiers and workers during these activities differ (Kaib, 1990; Traniello, 1981; Traniello and Busher, 1985).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Behavioral patterns of soldiers and workers during foraging differ in termites.
source: Termite soldiers are known to lay pheromone trails, to detect TFPs and to participate in foraging and field exploration in a number of termite species, though the behavioral patterns of soldiers and workers during these activities differ (Kaib, 1990; Traniello, 1981; Traniello and Busher, 1985).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Differences in sensitivity of termite workers and soldiers have not previously been addressed at the electrophysiological level.
source: Yet, differences in sensitivity of termite workers and soldiers have not previously been addressed at the electrophysiological level.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field prior to the current work.

claim: Caste-biased PsimOR14 expression and neocembrene sensitivity may represent olfactory information filtering adaptive to the different tasks of the two castes.
source: Caste-biased PsimOR14 expression and neocembrene sensitivity may represent olfactory information filtering adaptive to the different tasks of the two castes, as documented, for example, in ants (Caminer et al., 2023).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citation to a study in ants.

claim: Genus Prorhinotermes is the most basally situated termite taxon known to have a terpenoid component as part of its pheromone repertoire.
source: Genus Prorhinotermes is the most basally situated termite taxon known to have a terpenoid component as a part of its pheromone repertoire (Sillam-Dussès et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sillam-Dussès et al., 2009.

claim: The acquisition of terpenoid pheromone components is due to the evolution of terpene biosynthesis in basal Neoisoptera.
source: The acquisition of terpenoid pheromone components is undoubtedly due to the evolution of terpene biosynthesis in basal Neoisoptera, which has led to the fascinating diversity of defensive terpenoids produced by soldiers of Neoisoptera in their frontal gland (Gössinger, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gössinger, 2019.

claim: Some defensive terpenoids from the frontal gland gained a novel function of alarm pheromones via exaptation.
source: In line with general observations on pheromone evolution (Steiger et al., 2011), some of these defensive terpenoids from the frontal gland gained via exaptation a novel function of alarm pheromones (Dolejšová et al., 2014; Roisin et al., 1990; Šobotník et al., 2008; Šobotník et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Neocembrene occurs as a pheromone component in Prorhinotermes and in Nasutitermitinae.
source: Beside the occurrence of neocembrene in the sub-basal Prorhinotermes, it only occurs as a pheromone component in much later diverging representatives of the subfamily Nasutitermitinae (Bordereau and Pasteels, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bordereau and Pasteels, 2011.

claim: Insect ORs are frequently organized in tandem arrays.
source: Insect ORs are frequently organized in tandem arrays (e.g., Bohbot et al., 2007; McKenzie and Kronauer, 2018; Robertson and Wanner, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The genomic locus of PsimOR14 contains a likely tandem copy paralog of PsimOR15 gene.
source: Likewise, the genomic locus of PsimOR14 contains a likely tandem copy paralog of PsimOR15 gene.
evidence: This is based on genomic mapping.

claim: PsimOR14 and PsimOR15 transcripts are equally represented in worker antennal transcriptome.
source: The two genes share the gene architecture, and their transcripts are equally represented in worker antennal transcriptome, though PsimOR15 does not display the caste-biased expression.
evidence: This is based on transcript abundance data.

claim: PsimOR15 does not display caste-biased expression.
source: The two genes share the gene architecture, and their transcripts are equally represented in worker antennal transcriptome, though PsimOR15 does not display the caste-biased expression.
evidence: This is based on differential expression analysis.

claim: PsimOR15 is a candidate for potential pheromone receptor function.
source: Thanks to the close similarity of both genes, PsimOR15 is a candidate for potential pheromone receptor function.
evidence: This is speculation based on the similarity to PsimOR14.

claim: Termite OR sequences do not show conspicuous expansions analogous to 9-exon subfamily in ants.
source: In spite of the similarities in CHC roles in termites and ants, ranging from nestmate recognition to fertility signaling, termite OR sequences do not show any conspicuous expansions analogous to 9-exon subfamily in ants.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis of termite ORs.

claim: Queen pheromones in termites were identified in two species.
source: In termites, queen pheromones were so far only identified in two species (Dolejšová et al., 2022; Matsuura et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dolejšová et al., 2022 and Matsuura et al., 2010.

claim: Queen pheromones in termites are volatile and act as airborne signals via olfaction.
source: They are volatile and were shown to act as airborne signals via olfaction (Dolejšová et al., 2022); it is thus reasonable to expect a selective OR responsible for their detection.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dolejšová et al., 2022.

claim: It is reasonable to expect a selective OR responsible for detection of termite queen pheromones.
source: They are volatile and were shown to act as airborne signals via olfaction (Dolejšová et al., 2022); it is thus reasonable to expect a selective OR responsible for their detection.
evidence: This is speculation based on the nature of queen pheromones.
